subject: english-language
title: Cognition First
welcome_lead: Piaget argued thought precedes language. Walk through the stages and weigh cognition's role in acquisition.
meta_desc: Piaget's cognitive theory, schemas and object permanence in child language acquisition at A-Level.
final_note: You have placed cognition at the heart of acquisition — language fits the conceptual scaffold the child has built.

concepts.def: Jean Piaget argued language reflects cognitive development; children acquire concepts before the words for them.
The understanding (developed around 8 months) that objects exist when out of sight — a prerequisite for naming absent things.
Mental structures for organising experience; assimilation extends a schema, accommodation revises it.
Piaget's first stage (0-2 years), in which language begins to label sensorimotor experience.
Piaget's term for early self-directed speech that he viewed as cognitively immature; Vygotsky disputed this, seeing it as social.
Chomsky's nativism stresses innate grammar; Piaget's constructivism stresses cognitive construction through interaction with the world.

walkthroughs.body_html:
For Piaget the child cannot use a word like more meaningfully until the concept of quantity is in place.

Language acquisition tracks cognitive milestones: gone requires object permanence; before requires temporal ordering.

A toddler calls every four-legged animal doggy (assimilation into a dog-schema). On meeting a cat that meows, the schema accommodates and splits.

Overextension is a window onto cognitive categorisation in progress.

Chomsky's nativism explains the speed of syntax learning; Piaget's constructivism explains why semantics tracks cognitive development.

Modern approaches treat acquisition as the interaction of innate predispositions, cognitive growth and social scaffolding.

options: Concepts precede the words for them

Caregiver speech is irrelevant
Words always come before concepts

options: Overextension by assimilation
Underextension
Operant conditioning
A virtuous error in syntax

mcqs.q: What did Chomsky propose about language acquisition?
options: Chomsky said children learn language entirely by copying adults.
Chomsky said children should be taught grammar from age two.
Children possess an innate Language Acquisition Device — an inborn capacity for grammar — because exposure alone cannot account for how rapidly and uniformly children learn complex syntax.
It is the stage where children memorise long stories.

mcqs.q: How does Piaget's theory relate language to cognitive development?
options: Chomsky said children should be taught grammar from age two.

Language develops as a consequence of cognitive development — children must first develop concepts (object permanence, conservation) before they can express them linguistically. Cognition leads language.
Piaget was a behaviourist who emphasised reinforcement.
Piaget said language drives cognitive development.

mcqs.q: What is the telegraphic stage of child language development?
options: It is the stage when children first start using a telephone.
Around age 2-3, children produce short utterances containing content words but omitting function words and inflections (e.g. 'mummy gone shop').
Chomsky said children should be taught grammar from age two.
It is the stage where children memorise long stories.
